headings.title: Introduction and Physiological Renal Changes in Normal Pregnancy
headings.content: During a normal pregnancy, the maternal urinary system undergoes profound anatomical and physiological adaptations to accommodate the developing fetus and increased metabolic demands. One of the most prominent changes is systemic vasodilation and an increase in blood volume, which leads to a dramatic rise in the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) by as much as 50 percent compared to non-pregnant states. Consequently, serum markers such as creatinine and urea normally decrease, with typical normal values dropping to around 40 to 60 micromoles per liter for serum creatinine. Anatomically, hormonal influences, primarily progesterone, along with mechanical compression from the growing gravid uterus, cause dilation of the renal calyces, renal pelvis, and ureters, a condition known as physiological hydronephrosis, which is more commonly pronounced on the right side. This urinary stasis combined with increased excretion of glucose and amino acids creates an environment conducive to bacterial growth, raising the baseline risk for bacteriuria. Understanding these normal physiological adjustments is vital for Nigerian nursing students and clinicians, as failing to recognize that a creatinine level of 90 micromoles per liter might already indicate renal impairment in a pregnant woman can lead to delayed diagnosis and compromised maternal-fetal outcomes.

headings.title: Classification of Renal Diseases in Pregnancy
headings.content: Renal diseases in pregnancy encompass a spectrum of conditions that can either predate conception or develop de novo during gestation. Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is staged according to baseline GFR and proteinuria, and its presence significantly complicates the gestational journey depending on the baseline severity and etiology, such as diabetic nephropathy, lupus nephritis, or hypertensive nephrosclerosis. On the other hand, conditions like acute kidney injury (AKI) and de novo glomerular diseases may emerge acutely during pregnancy-specific complications. Preeclampsia is a major contributor to new-onset renal dysfunction in pregnant women, characterized by endothelial injury, glomerular endotheliosis, and significant proteinuria. Furthermore, pregnancy can sometimes unmask underlying, previously undiagnosed primary glomerulonephritis or exacerbations of systemic autoimmune disorders. For nursing professionals practicing in clinical environments across Nigeria, differentiating between chronic renal impairment predating pregnancy and acute pregnancy-induced renal insults is paramount for tailoring effective interventions, anticipating obstetric complications, and collaborating seamlessly with obstetricians and nephrologists.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Impact of Renal Impairment on Maternal-Fetal Outcomes
headings.content: Renal impairment during pregnancy poses substantial pathophysiological challenges that adversely impact both maternal and fetal well-being. When the kidneys fail to adequately filter waste products, toxins accumulate, and fluid and electrolyte homeostasis is disrupted. This internal milieu impairs vascular autoregulation, greatly elevating the risk of severe maternal hypertension, superimposed preeclampsia, and maternal pulmonary edema. From the fetal perspective, maternal renal insufficiency compromises placental perfusion, which can result in intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), oligohydramnios due to decreased fetal urine output, preterm birth, and increased rates of perinatal mortality. The severity of these adverse outcomes is directly correlated with the degree of maternal baseline renal dysfunction, the presence and severity of baseline hypertension, and the magnitude of proteinuria. Nurses monitoring patients with renal impairment must remain vigilant for subtle signs of deteriorating renal function, such as rapidly rising blood pressure, worsening pedal or facial edema, and decreasing urine output, ensuring timely escalation of care to protect both mother and child.

headings.title: Clinical Assessment and Diagnostic Evaluation
headings.content: Clinical assessment and diagnostic evaluation of renal disease in pregnant women require a meticulous approach that balances diagnostic accuracy with fetal safety. The evaluation begins with a thorough history, checking for a prior history of urinary tract infections, renal stones, autoimmune disorders, or chronic hypertension, followed by a physical examination focusing on blood pressure trends, volume status, and edema. Diagnostic investigations include serial serum creatinine, urea, and electrolyte levels, alongside 24-hour urine collection or spot protein-to-creatinine ratio to accurately quantify proteinuria. Urinalysis and urine culture are indispensable for ruling out or confirming urinary tract infections. Imaging studies must be selected cautiously; renal ultrasonography is the preferred imaging modality because it utilizes no ionizing radiation, effectively evaluating renal size, symmetry, and the presence of hydronephrosis or calculi. Nurses play a crucial role in preparing patients for these diagnostics, collecting accurate timed urine samples, monitoring vital signs, and offering reassurance to anxious mothers undergoing complex clinical evaluations.

headings.title: Antenatal and Nursing Management of Chronic Kidney Disease
headings.content: Antenatal and nursing management of Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) in pregnancy centers on multidisciplinary care aimed at preserving residual renal function and ensuring optimal fetal growth. Blood pressure control is the cornerstone of management; target blood pressures are typically maintained below 135/85 mmHg using safe antihypertensive agents such as methyldopa, labetalol, or nifedipine, while strictly avoiding teratogenic medications like ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs). Dietary modifications, often coordinated with a renal dietitian, involve balancing protein intake and managing sodium and potassium levels. Frequent antenatal visits are scheduled to monitor maternal kidney function, screen for superimposed preeclampsia, and perform serial fetal growth scans and biophysical profiles. Nurses provide essential education regarding medication adherence, dietary restrictions, early reporting of warning signs like severe headache or blurred vision, and emotional support. By maintaining close surveillance and fostering a therapeutic alliance, nurses help mitigate the risks associated with CKD and promote a successful pregnancy outcome.

headings.title: Management of Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) in Pregnancy
headings.content: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) in pregnancy is a critical medical and obstetric emergency that can occur due to pre-renal causes like severe hemorrhage or hyperemesis gravidarum, intra-renal causes such as acute tubular necrosis or severe glomerulonephritis, or post-renal causes like urinary tract obstruction. Conditions unique to pregnancy, such as septic abortion, placental abruption, postpartum hemorrhage, and thrombotic microangiopathies (like HELLP syndrome or hemolytic uremic syndrome), frequently precipitate AKI. Management requires immediate identification and correction of the underlying trigger, rigorous hemodynamic stabilization, and precise fluid balance management to avoid pulmonary edema while maintaining adequate placental perfusion. Renal replacement therapy, such as hemodialysis, may be instituted promptly if severe electrolyte imbalances, refractory acidosis, or fluid overload develop. Nurses play a frontline role in monitoring hourly urine output via indwelling urinary catheters, observing trends in serum creatinine and electrolytes, administering prescribed fluids or blood products safely, and remaining alert for signs of multi-organ failure.

headings.title: Urinary Tract Infections and Obstetric Complications
headings.content: Urinary tract infections (UTIs), ranging from asymptomatic bacteriuria to acute cystitis and severe pyelonephritis, are among the most common bacterial complications encountered during pregnancy. The physiological urinary stasis, ureteral dilation, and vesicoureteral reflux induced by pregnancy hormones make it easy for bacteria, most commonly Escherichia coli, to ascend and colonize the urinary tract. Asymptomatic bacteriuria must be aggressively screened for and treated with appropriate, pregnancy-safe antibiotics during routine antenatal visits because untreated bacteriuria progresses to acute pyelonephritis in up to 40 percent of cases. Pyelonephritis is a serious obstetric complication characterized by high fever, flank pain, nausea, and vomiting, which can trigger uterine contractions, preterm labor, maternal sepsis, and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Nursing care involves administering prescribed antibiotic therapy, ensuring adequate hydration, monitoring temperature and vital signs, educating patients on proper perineal hygiene and frequent bladder emptying, and watching for early signs of preterm labor.

headings.title: Intrapartum and Postpartum Nursing Care Considerations
headings.content: Intrapartum and postpartum care for women with renal disease requires careful interprofessional coordination to ensure maternal safety during delivery and the vulnerable puerperium. The timing and mode of delivery are planned collaboratively, taking into account fetal maturity, maternal renal function status, and blood pressure control. During the intrapartum period, continuous electronic fetal monitoring is essential due to the high risk of placental insufficiency and fetal distress. Fluid management must be meticulously balanced; excessive intravenous fluids can easily precipitate acute pulmonary edema in women with impaired renal clearance, while fluid restriction can compromise placental perfusion. In the postpartum period, the risk of hemorrhage, thromboembolism, and postpartum hypertension or preeclampsia remains high. Nurses must monitor lochia, assess blood pressure every few hours, track urine output, and educate breastfeeding mothers about medication safety, ensuring that prescribed antihypertensives or other renal medications are safe for lactation before discharge.
